body.text: Interpol, the international police organization, is a network through which the police forces of 196 countries share information. For decades, it showed what multilateral cooperation could achieve against terrorism, trafficking, and organized crime. That same network now offers authoritarian governments a cheap way to pursue their critics abroad. No government has learned to work the system more skillfully than China’s.

On November 30, Interpol’s General Assembly convenes in Hong Kong. It’s a special absurdity that the world’s police chiefs will be the guests of a state that uses Interpol to hunt its political opponents.

Sycophants will object that Hong Kong is not China. While that distinction died fully in 2020 with the National Security Law, at Interpol it never existed. Hong Kong is not a member in its own right, and its requests go through the same National Central Bureau in Beijing as the rest of China.

China has spent a decade abusing Interpol’s Red Notices, which are international alerts to law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, at the request of a member state.
A report published today, “The Red Notice Trap: How China and Hong Kong Turn Interpol Alerts into Instruments of Return,” sheds light on how the system works in practice.

Take China-born Singaporean businessman, known as “H.” He was detained by French officers in 2021 after Chinese prosecutors obtained a Red Notice accusing him of money laundering. On paper, his case looked to be one of ordinary economic crime.

Court records obtained by journalists told a different story. Chinese officials offered to cancel the notice and unfreeze his accounts if he gave evidence in an unrelated political investigation, a clear breach of Interpol’s rules. A Hong Kong national security official was also recorded discussing the same bargain. Jack Ma, the founder of Alibaba, telephoned to urge him to return. H says his sister was arrested to add yet more pressure.

Even when Interpol acts, it is often too late. Idris Hasan, a Uyghur activist, was arrested at the Casablanca airport in July 2021 on a Red Notice accusing him of terrorism. Within about three weeks Interpol had reviewed the notice and canceled it. Yet he was not released until February 12, 2025, some 43 months after his arrest.

These are not isolated incidents. By Beijing’s own count, it brought back more than 14,000 people from over 120 countries from 2014 to 2024. Only 79 of them were extradited. The rest came back through what officials call “persuasion to return,” which in lay terms means frozen assets, travel bans, and pressure on relatives at home.

Many of those 14,000 will be real criminals. That is part of the strategy, because floods of legitimate requests make the abusive ones hard to pick out. Interpol is badly underfunded and does not have the staff to keep pace with China.

China has worked hard to build a sophisticated, global network of oppression. It has secured extradition treaties with 10 EU member states and runs a network of unofficial police stations across the West. In June two men, one of them a Border Force officer, were jailed at the Old Bailey, a London court, for running a “shadow policing” operation against Hong Kong dissidents. Nobody is out of China’s reach.

As China’s power grows, few governments dare to confront the Chinese Communist Party directly. Interpol, ironically, is the place to start, as its own constitution forbids it from touching political cases.

That is why the General Assembly, despite all its controversies, is an opportunity for action. Member states will elect all seven members of the Commission for the Control of Interpol’s Files, the body that decides whether a notice stays or goes. Governments should back candidates whose independence is beyond question and vote the Commission the money and staff to do its job.

They should also demand figures. Interpol’s rules already allow it to suspend a country’s access to its databases for repeated abuse, but nobody outside its Lyon headquarters knows how many requests from each country it rejects or deletes, because Interpol does not publish those numbers. It must, with Hong Kong shown separately, so that member states can see who is abusing the system and how often.

Finally, where credible evidence emerges that a Red Notice is politically motivated, Interpol should be able to freeze it at once and should tell the courts of any country holding the person why it has done so. Idris Hasan might then have spent weeks in a Moroccan prison, and not years.

Hong Kong wants to be seen as a responsible partner in international law enforcement and can hardly object to any of this. Governments that take the rule of law seriously should arrive there with a list of candidates and a list of demands.
